core: The working definition of checks and balances: the mechanisms by which each branch of the federal government can limit the actions of the other branches, requiring them to work together (OpenStax / USA.gov framing)
The four central mechanisms, each stated factually in one line: veto and override, confirmation (advice and consent), judicial review, impeachment
Why the system exists: to prevent any one branch from dominating, attributed to the Federalist Papers
The system in motion: an original example tracing one check end to end
The honest note: checks can become gridlock, stated factually as a consequence of the supermajority rules
The honest framing: checks and balances as a machine for turning ambition into negotiation, attributed to Federalist 51's ambition-countering-ambition idea
supporting: Marbury v. Madison (1803) as the case that established judicial review, per the National Archives
The clause locations in the primary text: Article I Sections 2, 3, and 7; Article II Sections 2 and 4
NARA's framing that checks and balances was 'created to prevent any one branch of the Federal Government from becoming too powerful'
USA.gov's plain-language formulation of the checks (veto, confirmation, removal, judicial review)
Federalist No. 51's title and the sentence 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition'

claims.claim: Checks and balances is the system by which each branch of the federal government has the power to restrict the actions of the others, thus requiring them to work together; USA.gov states that the ability of each branch to respond to the actions of the other branches is the system of checks and balances.

Veto and override: under Article I, Section 7, a bill passed by both houses is presented to the president, who may sign it or return it with objections (the veto); Congress can then pass the bill into law over the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.

Confirmation: under Article II, Section 2, the president nominates ambassadors, Supreme Court justices, and other officers 'by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,' so the Senate confirms or rejects the president's nominees.

Judicial review: in Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall established the principle that courts determine the constitutionality of the actions of the other branches; the Court declared that 'a law repugnant to the Constitution is void.'

Impeachment: the House of Representatives has the sole power to formally charge (impeach) federal officials (Article I, Section 2); the Senate has the sole power to try impeachments, with conviction requiring two-thirds of members present (Article I, Section 3); removal applies to treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors (Article II, Section 4).

The purpose of checks and balances is to prevent any one branch from dominating; the National Archives describes the system as 'created to prevent any one branch of the Federal Government from becoming too powerful,' and the Federalist Papers argued for arranging the government so the branches check one another, with Federalist No. 51 stating that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'

The honest note, stated factually: because each check stops action unless the target yields or a supermajority forms (a veto stands unless two-thirds of both houses override it), the system can stall; when the branches are divided, commentators and political scientists describe that condition as gridlock.

The honest framing: Federalist No. 51's ambition-countering-ambition design means each branch's self-interest drives its checks, so the branches must negotiate to get anything done — checks and balances is a machine for turning ambition into negotiation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether gridlock is a design flaw or a feature of the checks-and-balances system.
positions: Checks require supermajorities or cooperation, so divided branches can stall legislation, nominations, and other action — a condition commentators and political scientists describe as gridlock.
The same difficulty is arguably the point: the framers preferred slow, deliberate action to domination by one branch, so stalemate is a feature of the design, not a bug.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the mechanism factually (a veto stands unless two-thirds of both houses override; a nomination fails without a Senate majority) and presents gridlock as an observed consequence of those rules, noting that it is a debated trade-off. The lesson takes no position on whether gridlock is desirable.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The constitutional basis of judicial review: the Constitution does not explicitly grant courts the power to strike down laws.
positions: Since Marbury v. Madison (1803), courts have exercised judicial review and declared laws repugnant to the Constitution void; NARA and OpenStax document this as an established power.
Scholars debate how firmly the text itself supports judicial review, since the power was established by the Court's own decision rather than by an explicit grant.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the history factually: the Supreme Court established judicial review in Marbury v. Madison (1803), and NARA describes it as an addition to the system of checks and balances. No interpretive advocacy; the debate over the textual basis is noted only in this packet.

Verified: the framers created 'a system of checks and balances by giving each of three branches of government the power to restrict the actions of the others, thus requiring them to work together'; the chief concern was increasing the authority of the national government 'while ensuring that it did not become too powerful'; Congress can be checked by the president's veto; a vetoed bill becomes law if it passes both houses again by two-thirds; Marbury v. Madison (1803) established the Supreme Court's authority to rule on the constitutionality of laws, a process called judicial review.
